A figure in invented, shining armor stands on a piece of floating ground, held up by cables that rise out of the frame. It looks like her own land, but it is borrowed ground.
You paid with real money. The skin is in your account, you use it in matches and the other players see it.
It looks like yours, and in large part it is.
Tomorrow it may change its look, lose the effect you liked or disappear along with the account, without anyone properly explaining why.
The promise of distinction remains nominally in the account, but no longer finds, in the world of the game, the fit that gave value to the investment of time, money and attention.<1>p. 104</1>

Once the account is terminated, the user will no longer have access to the account, nor to the associated data, nor to the Virtual Content, including in-game currency, and the consequence is definitive loss without refund whenever the landlord deems there was cause<1>p. 155</1>
Who would you complain to, and what would you complain about?

It is not only in games. An artificial intelligence assistant, an online store or a work app can work the same way, whenever what you use depends on an environment that the company maintains, updates, reorganizes and controls.
The criterion, therefore, is not the materiality of the medium nor the nomenclature used by the supplier, but the structural dependence of enjoyment on a governed environment.<1>p. 719</1>

The point, here, is not to gather digital examples under a single heading out of mere technological affinity, nor to suggest that every contemporary platform reproduces, with identical intensity, the same form of vulnerability, opacity or capture of enjoyment<1>p. 755</1>

In these places nothing stays still. Many changes are normal and part of the life of the service. Others are not, and the time, attention, reputation and money you put there do not show up on any receipt. When did this start to seem normal?
It allows us to recognize the sophisticated obvious: continuous digital services change, but they cannot change in just any way<1>p. 655</1>

Ordinary updates, regular curation, anti-abuse interventions and changes that do not reach the functional core of the enjoyment bundle remain within the normal field of performance and do not constitute relevant degradation by definition.<1>p. 430</1>

When did it become naturalized that time, attention, reputation, collection, bond and property can be captured and undone by design, without this being named with the weight it deserves and, above all, without generating the consequences it should generate?<1>p. 21</1>

What did you buy, after all?
Someone receives a gift box with a piece of armor inside. The piece reaches the hands of the buyer, but the ribbon on the box is a long cord that runs back to the store and does not come loose.

The most common scene is this one. You opened the game store, chose a skin and pressed the button that says buy. The money left your card and, a few seconds later, the skin appeared in your inventory, next to the others you already had.

The word on the button is not there by chance. In everyday Portuguese, and also in the Civil Code, to buy is to exchange money for a thing that becomes yours. Whoever buys expects the thing to stay, not to disappear without reason and to be usable for something. This holds even when you know the item is digital, because the word awakens this expectation on its own, like a shortcut the mind takes without thinking.

Both common sense and even the Brazilian Civil Code itself use the verb “to buy” in the sense of acquiring something that becomes “yours”, in the sense that minimum stability, permanence and some form of control over what was acquired are expected<1>p. 400-401</1>
Its classic structure is the exchange of a thing for a price<1>p. 400</1>
Even when one knows that it is a digital item, the language of purchase and sale automatically triggers this typical expectation and works as an interpretive shortcut.<1>p. 401</1>

The game reinforces this reading with another word, collection. Your inventory does not appear as a list of files, but as a collection, arranged for you to complete series, recognize what is rare, compare and display. Whoever collects keeps the story of each piece and builds, with what they gathered, a bond that lasts over time.

That is why, when an account is blocked or an item loses the function it had, the loss does not reach just a loose file. It reaches the whole collection, which only makes sense while the game keeps recognizing and showing those pieces the way you came to know them.

Collecting does not mean merely gathering items. It means ordering a collection, recognizing rarity, comparing value, preserving history, completing series, displaying belonging and building a relationship of continuity between subject and object.<1>p. 401</1>

Therefore, any account block, item removal, substantial alteration of functionality or architectural devaluation of the collection does not reach only a detachable digital unit. It reaches the intelligibility of the collection itself as a bundle of continued enjoyment, whose value depends on internal recognition, minimum stability and the preservation of the relationship between the consumer, their items and the ecosystem that gives them meaning.<1>p. 401</1>

Now comes what almost nobody does, which is opening the terms of use, the contract you accepted when you created the account. There the same skin does not appear as a purchase. It appears as virtual content, which the company offers through a limited and revocable license, tied to your account.

License, here, means permission to use. Revocable means that this permission can be withdrawn, and the contract itself warns that, if the account is terminated, the license is canceled at once. In other words, the screen speaks the language of purchase, while the contract speaks the language of conditional access, administered by the company.

The Terms of Service describe the same items as “Virtual Content” offered under an access license tied to the account <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>. The consequence is that what the interface presents as a “purchase”, the contractual instrument requalifies as conditional and institutionally administered access.<3>p. 401</3>

The service's own contractual framework gives shape to this arrangement by establishing that access to the Services, including the so-called Virtual Content, occurs through a limited and revocable license, conditioned on compliance with the Terms, and that the termination of the account entails automatic cancellation of the license and loss of access to the associated content<1>p. 408</1>
In plain language, this means that access to the ecosystem is structured as a conditional permission to use, and not as ownership of an autonomous good.<1>p. 408</1>

And there is a detail that works in your favor. The same terms that speak of a license recognize that there is virtual content tied to your account, made up of in-game currency, skins, emotes and other items. And they admit that you may have bought it, earned it or received it as a gift.

This helps prove that what you have exists and can be identified. The contract shows that the object is there, but it does not decide on its own which rules apply to it. And consumer law also calls a product what has no body, so the lack of a physical medium does not take the item out of protection.

Riot Games' Terms of Service expressly recognize a core of “Virtual Content” associated with the account, made up of in-game currency, skins, emotes, accessories and other items, and admit that this formation may occur through purchase, earning, gift or other internal dynamics of the ecosystem.<1>p. 575</1>
The clause helps prove the existence of the object. It does not exhaust its regime.<1>p. 575</1>

The legal definition of product in art. 3, §1, of the CDC<1><2>1</2></1> operates as a clause of scope that prevents escape from protective coverage when the object does not present itself in the form of a physical medium.<3>p. 411</3>
The law does not condition the product on corporeality, nor tie it to the image of the tangible thing delivered once and for all.<1>p. 574</1>

Maybe you think it is your fault, for not having read it. That is not the point. What happens is that the game itself guides your decision with a word that promises acquisition, while keeping in the contract a regime that does not match the ordinary meaning of buying.

And it is no use saying the information was there. Information can exist in the contract and still guide no one, when it is the screen that drives the experience at the moment of choice. You decide by the grammar of purchase, but you use what you bought by the grammar of the revocable license.

The point is not to assert that the consumer “did not read” or “did not understand”, but to recognize that the ecosystem itself organizes the decision through a sign that frames the relationship as a typical contract, while reserving, on the legal plane, a regime that does not coincide with the ordinary meaning of the verb “to buy”.<1>p. 401</1>

The relevant asymmetry is not merely a lack of information, since information may exist and, even so, not operate as practical guidance when the language of the interface governs the experience and stabilizes expectations in real time.<1>p. 401</1>

The result is an objective inequality of decoding and agency, because the consumer decides under the grammar of “buying”, but enjoyment takes place under the grammar of the “revocable license” associated with the account<1>p. 401-402</1>
So is the word buy forbidden?

This does not mean the word buy is illegal. The game can use the usual words, and nobody needs to change the button. The problem begins when nothing is left, behind the word, of minimum stability in what you bought. Then the comparison with a purchase becomes false, the expectation you rightly had is broken, and only then does the unlawful act appear, that is, something the law does not accept.

That is why the way out is not to forbid the word. It is to require the company to answer for the changes it makes, keeping a record of them, and to preserve an equivalent function when the change is legitimate.

[...] the consumer decides under the grammar of “buying”, but enjoyment takes place under the grammar of the “revocable license” associated with the account. This does not serve as grounds for asserting that the use of the word “buy” is, by itself and in isolation, unlawful.<1>p. 401-402</1>

The issue is that, without a core that respects the minimum stability of the good, even the superficial parallel becomes false and, therefore, leads to the breach of the legitimate expectation of enjoyment, only thus constituting unlawfulness.<1>p. 402</1>

It is not a matter of preventing the use of typical expressions, but of ensuring minimum fulfillment of the expectation by establishing responsibility for the auditability of changes and requiring the preservation of equivalent functionality in case of legitimate change.<1>p. 402</1>
What does your account hold besides the login?

To understand what you have, the best starting point is your account. It is not just a login and password. It is where your inventory, your progress, your player name and the signs by which others recognize you in the game are kept together. Characters, skins, emotes and in-game currency only work tied to it and cannot be taken outside.

That is why the account holds everything together. If someone breaks into your account, you need to open a ticket for the company to recover it, which shows that it is a record the company keeps and administers. And if the company terminates the account because it believes there was cause, you lose access to it and to the data tied to it. You also lose the virtual content, including the currency you paid for, and you lose it without a refund.

The contract also makes no distinction between someone who spent years gathering items and someone who just arrived. The account does not become more yours because it received ten thousand hours of dedication or money equivalent to a budget car.

The player's account in the Riot ecosystem offers a methodologically privileged example of an immaterial object of consumption in its most “infrastructural” form. It is not reduced to a login credential. It is the organizational point that holds the enjoyment bundle together, because it concentrates, in a single institutional record, the inventory of licensed virtual content, progression markers, social identifiers and the reputation signals by which the user's presence is read, displayed and recognized in the environment.<1>p. 408</1>

Champions, skins, emotes and in-game currency are part of the catalog of goods that only become enjoyable as an access license associated with the account, and not as things transportable outside it<1>p. 408</1>
In official guidance, Riot recognizes the possibility of a compromised account and states that, in that case, the user must open a ticket to recover it<1>p. 409</1>

Once the account is terminated, the user will no longer have access to the account, nor to the associated data, nor to the Virtual Content, including in-game currency, and the consequence is definitive loss without refund whenever the landlord deems there was cause<1>p. 155</1>
The contract does not distinguish someone who spent years accumulating signs of belonging from someone who has just joined<1>p. 153</1>
because it received ten thousand hours of dedication over fifteen years, nor because it received investment comparable to the cost of a budget car<1>p. 154</1>
What does a subway turnstile have to do with your skin?

What you bought exists and has value, but it can only be used inside a turnstile, like the ones at a subway station, and whoever controls the turnstile is the platform. It decides who gets through, who stays and on what conditions, both through the contract and through technology.

The contract tries to convince you that the turnstile is everything, as if your payment bought only a tolerance to stay inside, which can be withdrawn at any moment. But the turnstile changes the conditions of use and does not erase what you bought.

The IOC, as the concretization of the immaterial product in the sense of art. 3, §1, of the CDC<1><2>1</2></1>, appears here not as neutral content, but as a commodity form whose enjoyment is subordinated to contractual and technological turnstiles<3>p. 186</3>

And the account, far from being a good of the consumer, is described as a private space whose “right” of use comes down to a personal and revocable permission, which is not to be confused with ownership.<1>p. 153</1>
What one buys, in practice, is a tolerance of access that can be withdrawn<1>p. 153</1>

A turnstile at the entrance of a garden. Inside, the figure in shining armor. The turnstile is not at the exit, it stands in the path of whoever wants to stay inside. The figure exists and belongs to whoever bought it, and the turnstile only controls the conditions of use.

And what you bought does not stop existing just because you cannot hold it in your hand. The company itself defines in the contract what virtual content is, names the items and ties them to your account. It also admits that you can obtain this content by buying it, earning it in missions or receiving it as a gift. In doing so, it recognizes that there is a set of things there that can be identified, and this recognition dismantles the idea that nothing was delivered.
The company expressly defines “Virtual Content” as a set that includes in-game currency, champions, skins, emotes, accessories and other items associated with the account<1>p. 566</1>
and admits that this content may be obtained not only through classic purchase, but also through earning, reward, gift or other internal dynamics of the ecosystem<1>p. 566</1>

First, because it shows that the contractual design itself recognizes an identifiable core of enjoyment associated with the account, which dismantles the puerile thesis of the legal nonexistence of the object.<1>p. 566</1>
<1>Law</1>Digital goods

Things without a body can also be goods. Information organized on a computer can have its own usefulness and be part of your interests, even when it is not immediately worth money. Once recognized as a good, it can be used, enjoyed, passed on and protected by law.

This starting point is indispensable. Without it, the crude idea would prevail that everything you cannot hold in your hand is light, disposable and can vanish at the mere will of the seller. But it does not settle everything. Knowing that the skin is a good still does not say what happens when the platform changes the game or tampers with the item's function. Nor does it say what applies when the platform decides on its own, over time, how the item can be used.

Digitally organized information may take on its own usefulness, become part of the subject's sphere of interests and, for that reason, be treated as a legally relevant incorporeal good, with or without immediate economic content<1>p. 565</1>
It is also a real gain of this framework to recognize that, once admitted as goods, these assets become susceptible to appropriation, circulation, enjoyment and protection<1>p. 565</1>

This starting point is correct and indispensable. Without it, the debate on continuous digital consumption would remain hostage to the crude fiction according to which everything that cannot be held in the hand would be legally light, dissolvable and disposable at the mere will of the supplier.<1>p. 565</1>

The insufficiency would not lie in the inability of this framework to recognize the asset, but in the fact that, even recognizing appropriation and circulation, it does not exhaust the conflicts of continuous enjoyment, unilateral mutability and functional governance in a platform environment<1>p. 566</1>
<1>Governed enjoyment bundle</1>

So what, exactly, do you have? It is not just an image stuck onto the character. It is a set of things the skin lets you do and be inside the game. With it you play the match, appear to others, complete the collection and say something about who you are in that place.

Each of these things depends on the game continuing to work in a certain way. The skin needs the game to remain able to render the model, the effects and the animations, which change with every update. And what it means depends on other players seeing and recognizing it. That is why, more than a static thing, what you have is a position of use that the platform maintains and keeps adjusting over time.

The consumer does not buy merely an “image” attached to the character. They acquire a position of enjoyment that is only realized if the game environment remains able to render models, effects, animations and interfaces that are reconfigured with each cycle of patches and system adjustments<1>p. 439</1>
From this operator, the object can be described as a bundle of functionalities and meanings administered over the course of the relationship<1>p. 426</1>

The IOC does not behave as a “good” merely by virtue of an isolated functional utility, but as a functional and semiotic bundle, in which enjoyment depends on operations of public legibility and collective recognition.<1>p. 252</1>
Enjoyment ceases to be a simple initial enablement and becomes a position sustained within the ecosystem<1>p. 426</1>
Is the skin money in a drawer or water in a pipe?

Money kept in a drawer is a stock. It stays there, still, and tomorrow it is still money. Water running through a pipe is a flow, because it only reaches your faucet while someone keeps the network working. The skin is more like the water.

Its value is not stored in a corner that is yours alone. It depends on servers running, on connection and on an environment the company maintains every day. So much so that the company itself publishes a page showing whether the service is working. When the game goes down, the skin stays in the account, but at that moment it is useless, because the place where it works has stopped.
The use value of the bundle, in this condition, is not stock, it is flow. It requires continuity of servers, institutional connectivity and maintenance of the environment.<1>p. 409</1>
Riot maintains an official service status page, with current messages and a history of incidents<1>p. 409</1>

When the service becomes unavailable, it is not only access that fails, but the virtual content itself loses immediate usefulness, because the environment that makes it enjoyable stops operating.<1>p. 409</1>
On the left, a drawer with still coins. On the right, a transparent pipe with running water and a piece of armor carried by the current. If the faucet closes, the piece stops and loses its shine.

With all of this together, it becomes clear why the expression revocable license deserves suspicion. It gives the impression that nothing was delivered and that everything can evaporate without consequence. But if there is an item that can be identified, tied to your account and used in the game, there is something the law needs to take seriously. And this holds even if the contract speaks of it in the words of a precarious thing.

it sets aside, from the outset, the semantic fraud of the “revocable license” as a formula capable of evaporating everything that has already been economically incorporated into the user's sphere<1>p. 566</1>

If there is an identifiable virtual object, associated with the account and enjoyed within the ecosystem, there is legal relevance to be taken seriously, even if the platform tries to cover it with a vocabulary of precariousness.<1>p. 566</1>
<1>Immaterial Object of Consumption (IOC)</1>

Brazilian law had already left room for this. In 1990, the Brazilian Consumer Protection Code (Código de Defesa do Consumidor, CDC) said that a product is any good, material or immaterial. The door was open for goods that circulate without a body and depend on technical conditions maintained all the time. But the way of thinking about the product remained tied to the physical object, or to a delivery that begins and ends in an instant.

It was like a plot of land the law had marked out and that was left empty. The Immaterial Object of Consumption is the building raised on that land. It is the legal category for the case in which what you consume depends, structurally, on an environment the platform administers, adjusts and can change.

When this is the case, there is an immaterial product in the sense of consumer law. The service does not vanish from the picture, because it appears as the way the company maintains, updates and shapes what you bought. That is why the old dispute over whether the case is one of product or service loses force. The question that matters becomes how the company organizes the continuous delivery of what it sold and whether this way of supplying preserves or spoils what you acquired.
A product is any good, movable or immovable, material or immaterial<1>p. 24</1>

Article 3, §1, of the Consumer Protection Code already contains the normative opening necessary for the recognition of goods that circulate without a stable corporeal medium and whose enjoyment depends on continuous technical and organizational conditions.<1>p. 24</1>

It is necessary to recognize, however, that this expansibility of Brazilian Consumer Law has been held back by a strictly material ontology, which insists on reducing the product to the delivery of a physical medium or of a discrete and finalizable performance<1>p. 24</1>

The Immaterial Object of Consumption (IOC) presents itself, in this sense, as the definitive subdivision of a plot of land that the legislator of 1990 had already marked out, although contemporary doctrine has kept it in the condition of a vacant lot.<1>p. 24-25</1>
What matters is recognizing situations in which the economically enjoyed utility depends structurally on an environment administered, modulated and made mutable by private governance<1>p. 717</1>

What is asserted is that, whenever the consumed utility presents itself as a position of enjoyment sustained by continuous private governance, there will be an immaterial product in a legally relevant sense for the application of art. 3, § 1, of the CDC<1><2>1</2></1>.<3>p. 718</3>

The performance does not disappear, but appears as a mode of sustaining, updating and shaping the object of consumption itself. Therefore, the old question of whether the case involves a product or a service, taken in an exclusionary key, loses much of its analytical usefulness. The problem becomes the structure of supply and the way it organizes, preserves or degrades the acquired experience.<1>p. 718</1>
In how many ways does an item have value inside the game?

Inside a game, what you buy can take quite different forms, and it is worth knowing which one yours is. There is what is valued for its appearance, like the skin, which shows something to others and marks your place in the game. And there is what is valued as a path, like an event pass, in which you do not receive a ready prize, but the right to travel a track of goals and rewards.

There is also what secures your entry and your stay, like the account, which in practice works as a position that can be withdrawn. There are functions, like permissions and conveniences of use that are part of what you pay for. There is time, with seasons, deadlines and items that only come back to the store now and then, or never again. And there is reputation, the recognition the game itself measures, for example by your conduct, and that can lock rewards when it drops.

In real life these forms mix, and a limited edition skin is valued at the same time for its appearance and for its time. Separating one from another helps to see what exactly was affected when something changes, even if the item is still there.

The first category is that of cosmetic-ornamental objects. They are IOCs whose utility is not exhausted in functional performance attributes, since it incorporates symbolic value realized as distinction, belonging and recognition in the ecosystem.<1>p. 489</1>
The second category is that of progression objects.<1>p. 489</1>

A first example, typical of a progression object, is the event pass, in which the acquisition is not directed at a ready result, but at access to a metered trajectory of milestones and rewards<1>p. 491</1>
The third category is that of access and permanence objects.<1>p. 489</1>
These are IOCs marked by intense dependence on account, credentials and eligibility, so that enjoyment takes, in practice, the form of a revocable position<1>p. 489</1>

The fourth category is that of functionality objects. They are instrumental capabilities made available to the consumer under technical and normative parameters administered by the supplier, such as permissions of use, convenience utilities, configuration possibilities and conversion capabilities<1>p. 490</1>

The fifth category is that of time objects. It covers temporal structures that condition when, for how long and within which windows enjoyment may occur, such as validity regimes, seasons, availability cycles and frequency limits.<1>p. 490</1>

In operational language accessible to the public, certain categories of skins are treated as “legacy” or “limited”, with variations as to whether or not they return to the store and under which conditions, so that the symbolic utility of what was acquired also comes to depend on an institutionally administered temporality<1>p. 491</1>
The sixth category is that of reputation objects. They correspond to positions of recognition instituted by the ecosystem through metrics, validation criteria and visibility devices.<1>p. 490</1>

The honor system operates as a mechanism of comparable and socially intelligible recognition, but, at the same time, as everyday discipline, since behavior penalties can lock reputational progression and affect, in practical terms, access to rewards associated with loot crafting<1>p. 492</1>

The proposed categories neither eliminate the complexity of the ecosystem nor intend to reduce concrete objects to a single type. They provide comparable language to break down hybrid arrangements into controllable dimensions and to locate, with precision, which aspects were affected by a relevant modulation.<1>p. 492</1>
This typology is deliberately internal to the games laboratory and is not offered as a general classification of platforms.<1>p. 489</1>
Does your case answer yes to the four questions?

Not everything digital falls into this category, and it is good to know this before you complain. What decides is not that the item is digital nor the name the company gives it. It is how much what you use depends on an environment the platform governs. Four questions help to see this, and your case needs to answer yes to all of them.

The first is what was promised. It is not enough to say that some content was available. You need to say which utility was sold, that is, what the skin was supposed to let you do and mean, and this cannot be drawn from slogans or ornamental lists.

The second is whether the purchase opened a position that lasts. In continuous consumption, buying is not receiving a package and that is it. It is gaining a place in the game that needs to keep existing for the thing to be of use.

The third is whether the platform really governs that place. It is not enough for there to be technology along the way. There need to be internal rules, choices about what appears and punishments that shape your use and bring consequences for you.

The fourth is whether the thing can get worse without disappearing. This is the case in which access continues, but what you had is downgraded, emptied or reorganized against what was promised. A one-day instability or a neutral adjustment on the screen does not count.
The criterion, therefore, is not the materiality of the medium nor the nomenclature used by the supplier, but the structural dependence of enjoyment on a governed environment.<1>p. 719</1>

As a filter, it defines what enters and what remains outside the field of application, preventing any digital relationship with an appearance of continuity from being absorbed by the category and also preventing the supplier from expelling the conflict from the CDC through strategic labeling<1>p. 428</1>

The relevant question is not whether there was “content” available at some moment, but which utility was economically offered in terms of functionalities and meanings that, under the IOC regime, constitute what was acquired.<1>p. 428</1>
The criterion is not satisfied with ornamental lists of functionalities nor with generic advertising slogans.<1>p. 428</1>
In continuous consumption, the acquisition inaugurates a position in the ecosystem and not a delivery exhausted in an instant.<1>p. 428</1>

The filter here is decisive, since the presence of technical mediation in a trivial sense is not enough. What matters is the existence of internal criteria and executive mechanisms that structurally shape the experience of enjoyment and distribute consequences to the consumer.<1>p. 428</1>
It is a matter of delimiting the zone in which enjoyment continues to exist formally, but is downgraded, emptied or reconfigured<1>p. 429</1>

The qualification roadmap must require the demonstration of a pattern of degradation that is not to be confused with ordinary variations, occasional instabilities or neutral interface adjustments.<1>p. 429</1>
Application is not decided by technological intuition nor by automatic deference to the contract, but by the cumulative presence of verifiable elements of the regime<1>p. 429</1>
Does every annoyance with the game become a right?

And not every annoyance becomes a right. This category does not serve to turn any discomfort of digital use into a loss the law repairs, nor to condemn every technical choice of the company. An update, a change on the screen or a new order in the game's lists are not unlawful in themselves. What counts is serious and lasting worsening, recognizable by criteria, that reaches the core of what was sold, even when access continues.

There are also cases that are left out from the start. A service that happens once and ends there, without a position that lasts, follows the ordinary rules for services. A platform that only works as a shop window, without really governing what you use, also tends to be left out. And a change in appearance only, when symbolic value was not part of the core of what was sold, as a rule is not enough.

There are also cases in which the core of the problem is something else, like an undue charge, an occasional defect, an isolated misleading ad or an offer that was not honored. Then the usual consumer law tends to resolve it, without needing this category, and you remain protected along that path.

Recognizing it means treating as legally relevant the elements that define the consumer's permanence in the regime of enjoyment, without converting mere ordinary discomforts into legal losses<1>p. 428</1>
The IOC filter cannot ignore the structural features of platform-governed consumption nor, at the opposite extreme, aim to capture each and every discomfort of digital use<1>p. 429</1>
The category neither expands the unlawful act indefinitely nor moralizes technical choices.<1>p. 426</1>

The reconfigurability of the environment does not turn any update, interface adjustment, ranking change or ordinary curation choice into unlawfulness. What becomes legally relevant is significant, persistent degradation recognizable by criteria, the kind that alters the core of the economically offered utility or structurally downgrades the conditions of enjoyment that gave meaning to the acquisition.<1>p. 426</1>
The first limit is occasional access without a sustained position of enjoyment.<1>p. 433</1>
The second limit is the case in which the platform works as a channel or shop window, but does not govern, in structural terms, the acquired utility<1>p. 434</1>
The third limit concerns situations in which symbolic or semiotic value is functionally accessory and is not part of the core of the promised enjoyment bundle.<1>p. 434</1>
Therefore, as a rule, predominantly aesthetic changes fall outside the reach of the concept<1>p. 434</1>

The fifth limit is the case in which the core of the conflict is something else, such as a classic occasional defect, undue charge, localized misleading advertising or specific nonperformance of an offer. In these cases, common consumer law dogmatics tends to resolve the dispute with no real gain in mobilizing the IOC.<1>p. 435</1>

Why does this category make so much difference? Because, when a legal criterion for a loss is missing, it becomes hard to show it, prove it and hold someone accountable for it. And this void does not stay still. It becomes room for the company to profit.

A rule whose fine is almost never applied shows the mechanism. If enforcement is rare and punishment is unlikely, the risk stops acting as a brake and acquires a price, as if it were just another operating cost. This is how every lasting gap tends to become a business model. Legally qualifying what you lose is the first step for that loss to be seen and claimed.

When categories capable of making certain losses legally visible, of naming, demonstrating and imputing them, are lacking, the space of irresponsibility does not remain neutral and comes to function as a margin for optimization.<1>p. 25</1>
When enforcement is rare and sanction is unlikely, risk ceases to act as a brake and comes to be priced, as if it were merely an operating cost.<1>p. 25</1>
It produces predictable institutional effects, because every stable dogmatic gap tends to be converted into a business model.<1>p. 25</1>
What can you demand?
<1>Information needs to be good for something</1><2>Information needs to be good for something</2>
When the information exists, but does not guide?

When the platform trades clarity for excess text, scatters information across different places, breaks the path of whoever tries to understand or offers transparency for show only. This is the case of important rules buried in a huge contract, in FAQs nobody finds or in patch notes nobody can connect to what happened to your item.
What information must the platform give?
Information that truly serves, that helps you decide and that can be checked later, if there is a dispute. Information that exists somewhere, but guides no one, does not fulfill this duty.
How to show what was informed and what was missing?

What was shown to you, at what moment, with what prominence and through which channel. And whether, the way everything was organized, it was possible to understand what mattered in order to buy, to stay or to react.
What to ask for when the information failed?

That the platform correct the way it informs and make visible what matters. That it present what it actually displayed. And that it restore what you lost because of the lack of clarity. Depending on the case, the failure may be treated as a defect in the quality of the information or as an abusive practice. It may even lead to the invalidity of clauses that contradict what you had reason to expect.
Is the question whether you read the contract?
The discussion is not about whether you read the contract or not. It is about whether, the way the information was organized, it served to guide your decision.

Whenever the platform substitutes legibility with textual excess, strategic dispersion, fragmentation of informational paths or merely performative transparency, there will be inadequacy in the duty to inform.<1>p. 744</1>

Information, under the CDC, does not fulfill its function merely because it exists somewhere, nor because it was deposited in lengthy documents, cross-references, FAQs or update histories that the consumer will hardly locate, understand and connect to the impact<1>p. 641</1>
The corresponding duty of supply is to provide materially adequate information, useful for the decision and verifiable at a later moment of controversy.<1>p. 744</1>

The minimum required proof calls for identification of what was shown, at what moment, with what salience, through which channels and to what extent this organization allowed the consumer to understand what was legally relevant in order to adhere, remain or react.<1>p. 744</1>

The legal qualification tends to apply as a defect in the informational quality of the supply, an abusive practice by functional obscuring and, depending on the case, grounds for the invalidity of clauses or limitations incompatible with the legitimately formed expectation.<1>p. 744</1>

The possible institutional consequence includes a duty to correct the communicational arrangement, reinforcement of useful transparency, orders to display and restoration of the enjoyment affected by decisional opacity.<1>p. 744</1>
The point is not to assert that the consumer “did not read” or “did not understand”<1>p. 401</1>

Does the law already have an answer?

A contemporary building seen in cross-section, supported by an earlier foundation, already marked out and ready to receive its structures. The blue highlights the immaterial building and the line reveals the continuity with the foundation. The 1990 milestone stays in the HTML caption, with no numbers inside the image. The scene of the reduced class schedule is reserved to illustrate the degradation of the service, instead of the opening of this chapter.

Maybe you are thinking that a new law is missing, just for games and digital platforms. That is not quite it. What is missing, in most cases, is reading the law that already exists with the right eyes.

The Immaterial Object of Consumption does not call for a separate system, with its own rules for the digital world. It is an update of the reading that already fits within the Brazilian Consumer Protection Code (Código de Defesa do Consumidor, CDC) and the principles of the Federal Constitution that ground it. In other words, the law already had the tools, and what was missing was pointing them at the right place.

Instead of proposing an autonomous regulatory microsystem for “electronic games” or “digital platforms”, what is being proposed is a demonstration that the Immaterial Object of Consumption is a form of interpretive updating that, in dogmatic terms, is already internal to the CDC itself and derived from the constitutional principles that inform it<1>p. 36</1>
It is not a matter of inventing a new code nor of forcibly grafting a foreign regime onto the legal text.<1>p. 549</1>
The CDC already offers sufficient language to face this problem, provided one accepts that, in continuous digital consumption, to govern the environment is to govern enjoyment itself.<1>p. 550</1>
<1>Law</1>Consumer vulnerability
Consumer law starts from a fact it recognizes itself, that the consumer is the vulnerable party in the relationship.

In digital environments, this vulnerability takes on a form of its own. It becomes tied to signs, to screens and to private criteria that decide what appears and how each thing can be used. It is from this specific form of fragility that stronger duties of transparency, loyalty and information arise for whoever supplies.

From this perspective, it is argued that the factual vulnerability of the consumer, expressly recognized in art. 4, I, of the CDC<1><2>1</2></1>, takes on in digital environments a form of its own, linked to mediation by signs, interfaces and private criteria of visibility and enjoyment<3>p. 34</3>

[...] in dogmatic terms, the vulnerability intrinsic to immaterial objects of consumption as an interpreted dimension of the factual vulnerability of art. 4, I, of the CDC<1><2>1</2></1>, justifying reinforced duties of transparency, loyalty and information<3>p. 183</3>
What if a course cut half its classes?

A course that, in the middle of the semester, cuts half its classes and keeps charging the same price does what anyone would think is wrong. And consumer law agrees, because it considers void the clause that lets the supplier change on its own the content or quality of what it sells after the contract is made.

On platforms, this cut rarely comes under that name. Nobody announces they will cut classes. It shows up as smaller reach, performance downgraded little by little, functions that keep disappearing, tighter limits or use that gets more expensive to yield the same thing. The label and the price stay the same, while the delivery shrinks. The logic, however, is the same as the course.

If continuity is the normal regime, the enjoyed utility stabilizes as an expectation that the level of delivery will be maintained, and not as an expectation of formal access to a service that can be reconfigured at the supplier's convenience. That is why the CDC treats unilateral modification of content or quality as nullity.<1>p. 479</1>
The example he offers, of the supplier that reduces classes while keeping the same price <1>Nunes</1><2>(Nunes, 2018, [p. 508-509])</2>, works as an objective yardstick for platforms.<3>p. 480</3>

The reduction rarely appears as an explicit cut of “classes”, but it may manifest as loss of reach, persistent downgrading of performance, cumulative restriction of functionalities, compression of limits, reordering of visibility or structural changes that raise the cost of enjoying the same utility. The logic is the same. The label and the price are kept, and the delivery of value is downgraded.<1>p. 480</1>

This does not mean nothing can change. In contracts that last for years, change is part of the deal, because the conditions of the world change. What is expected is that changes serve to maintain the level and quality of what you use, and not to swap what you bought, in silence, for a version that is worth less.

Good faith, which is the requirement of loyalty between the parties, goes beyond what is written in the contract. It creates duties of care, cooperation and maintenance. That is why, when the company says the change was just an update, an adjustment or an evolution of the service, the conversation does not end there. What matters is showing that the essence of what you bought was preserved, and not the size of the technical complexity.

[...] and concludes that “the capacity for adaptation, for cooperation between contracting parties, for continuation of the contractual relationship is essential, basic here” [...] This formulation provides the fine fit for functional value equivalence: changes may be admissible and even necessary, provided they are oriented toward maintaining the potential and quality that structure the enjoyed utility, and not toward the silent substitution of the object with a less valuable version<1>p. 479</1>

The consequence is plain, since, if continued performance exposes the consumer to risks of technical obsolescence, compatibility mutations and structural reconfigurations, good faith must require care, cooperation and maintenance as duties of preserving functional equivalence<1>p. 479</1>

Whenever the platform invokes “update”, “adjustment” or “evolution of the service” to justify persistent changes, the core of the debate must fall on the demonstration of substantial preservation of the enjoyment bundle, and not on the rhetoric of complexity.<1>p. 480</1>
<1>Law</1>Software Law
There is even a specific law for computer programs, from 1998. It does not deal only with who owns the program and how it is licensed. It also creates duties for whoever sells.

Under the law, the license contract, the invoice and the packaging must state, in an easy-to-read way, for how long the version sold works technically. And, during that period, the supplier must guarantee the technical services that keep the program working properly, even if it stops selling that version. In other words, the supplier's responsibility for functioning over time has existed in the law for decades.

Law No. 9,609/1998 <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [1998])</2> does not describe only exclusivity and licensing as an enclosure of utilities, but structures positive duties of the supplier linked to the technical life cycle of the software.<3>p. 51</3>

Art. 7 requires that the license contract, the tax document and the media and packaging indicate, in an easily legible way, the technical validity period of the version marketed, and art. 8 converts this period into an obligation to ensure complementary technical services relating to the proper functioning of the program during the technical validity, including when it is withdrawn from commercial circulation<1>p. 51</1>
<1>Law</1>Economic order

What about the company's freedom to do business? It exists and is protected, but it is not a sovereignty without limits. Since the 1988 Federal Constitution, free enterprise goes hand in hand with human dignity and with social values.

Consumer protection, in fact, is at the same time a fundamental right and a principle of the economic order itself. This is enough to frame private forms of government, like those of platforms, that produce broad and repeated effects on your experience, even though they are not the State. Innovating, owning the technology or having market freedom do not give license to escape all scrutiny and all responsibility.

Economic activity, in the 1988 model, is not organized as a space of unrestricted patrimonial sovereignty, because free enterprise appears from the republican foundation bound to the dignity of the human person and to the social values that shape it.<1>p. 504</1>

Consumer protection as a fundamental right and principle of the economic order already offers sufficient grounds to frame, without artificiality, private forms of government that produce broad and repeated effects on the experience of enjoyment, even though they are not to be confused with state power.<1>p. 502</1>
Free enterprise, innovation and technological ownership do not operate as safe-conducts for unauditability, shielded irresponsibility or contractual immunization of the supplier.<1>p. 512</1>
<1>Law</1>Horizontal effect of fundamental rights

Fundamental rights are those the Constitution guarantees to all people, like freedom and equality. For a long time they were thought of as protection against the State. Today it is recognized that they also apply in relations between private parties, and that is what the expression horizontal effect means.

This matters because the power that weighs on you does not always come from the government. A company can organize, on a large scale, your access, your stay, your visibility, your reputation and even your chances to prove and to contest. It can also harm your freedom and your equality. And the freedom to contract cannot serve as a screen to hide such unequal relationships.

The horizontal effect of fundamental rights ceases to seem an abstract theoretical question when one observes that, in contemporary private relations, relevant subjection no longer comes only from the State. It also emerges from private centers of power capable of organizing access, permanence, visibility, reputation, proof and contestation on a scale sufficient to affect, structurally, the practical freedom and material equality of the subject bound by the relationship.<1>p. 512</1>
In such contexts, private autonomy cannot function as a screen to shield materially asymmetrical arrangements<1>p. 512</1>

The key lies in recognizing that, in contemporary society, relevant violations of fundamental rights come not only from the State, but also from private subjects endowed with economic, informational and organizational power<1>p. 24</1>
<1>Law</1>Social function of intellectual property

The Constitution protects inventions, trademarks and other creations. But it ties this protection to a goal, which is the social interest and the technological and economic development of the country. Exclusivity is not an end in itself.

That is why owning the work is not enough, on its own, to justify changing what you use without limit, deciding in secret or punishing with no chance of contesting. Intellectual property receives from the Constitution a frame with a purpose, and not a blank check. The company remains the owner of the game, but exercises this right within that frame.

Nor does it stay outside. In practice, intellectual property helps build the environment itself, because it is through it that the platform defines what can be accessed, kept, changed, withdrawn and contested.
In dealing with industrial property, art. 5, XXIX does not grant a self-justified patrimonial prerogative, nor does it protect exclusivity as an end in itself.<1>p. 702</1>

On the contrary, it expressly subordinates the legal guarantee of the privilege over industrial inventions and the protection of industrial creations, trademarks, company names and other distinctive signs to the social interest and the technological and economic development of the Country<1>p. 702</1>
The infraconstitutional framework of patrimonial intellectual property does not, therefore, receive a constitutional blank check; it receives a purposive frame.<1>p. 702</1>

Thus, the mere ownership of an IP right is not enough to legitimize, by itself, unilateral mutability of enjoyment, decisional opacity, uncontestable private sanction or destruction of utilities incorporated into the bond of continuous consumption.<1>p. 702-703</1>
It operates, in practice, as part of the legal infrastructure through which the platform defines what can be accessed, kept, altered, withdrawn, audited and contested.<1>p. 680</1>

They do not operate merely as patrimonial shields detached from the consumption experience, but as legal techniques for organizing the very environment in which enjoyment becomes possible, recognizable and economically exploitable.<1>p. 681</1>

What if the game shuts down? One day the company may end the service or switch off the servers for good. Even so, the fact that everything is stored in its structure does not turn your history, your collection, your progress and your reputation into worthless things that can simply vanish.

The company has the right to end or reorganize the business, but this right does not include erasing everything without any care for those who were inside. If the end is inevitable, the exit needs to come with some care, as far as possible. It may mean keeping the service running in another way, letting you take what is yours elsewhere, restoring what was lost or passing the operation on.

There is already, within IP itself, internal resistance to the idea that every immaterial bond can be dissolved by a simple dispositive decision of the owner. [...] This limit takes on a particularly sharp outline in cases of termination of activities, discontinuation of services or definitive shutdown of servers.<1>p. 709</1>

Histories, libraries, progressions, projected identities, reputational positions and long-term investments cannot be treated as residues without density merely because they are technically housed in someone else's infrastructure.<1>p. 709</1>

The right to exploit, terminate or reorganize economic activity is not to be confused with a supposed right to annihilate, without duties of transition, preservation or transfer, the functional enjoyment already stabilized in the consumer's sphere.<1>p. 709</1>

If the termination of the service is unavoidable, the constitutional order requires that it be reconciled, as far as technically and legally possible, with solutions of continuity, portability, functional restoration, assignment of the operation or other suitable measures<1>p. 709</1>
<1>Law</1>Legal framework for games

Since 2024, Brazil has had a law that recognizes electronic games as an economic and cultural activity with importance of its own. It includes games downloaded or played by streaming over the internet, and makes clear that gaming is not a minor pastime nor a matter beyond the reach of the law.

The law guarantees the freedom to create, sell and exploit games, but under the Constitution and the laws in force. And it says that games must respect fundamental rights, consumer protection, the full protection of children and adolescents and the privacy and personal data of those who play. That is why it is not an anything-goes with a modern face.

A sufficient milestone to record this fact is Law 14,852/2024 <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2024]b)</2>, taken here as a reference of institutional recognition of the electronic games industry as an economic and cultural activity with relevance of its own.<3>p. 493</3>

[...] it regulates its central economic chain — manufacture, import, sale, development and commercial use — and provides a normative definition of what counts as an electronic game, including interactive audiovisual works developed as computer programs, devices and accessories, and software consumed by download or streaming<1>p. 543</1>

The law affirms the freedom of manufacture, import, sale, development and commercial use of electronic games, but does so with express reference to art. 173 of the Constitution<1><2>2</2></1> and to the legislation in force.<3>p. 544</3>

The framework organizes the sector institutionally through principles and guidelines and, at its core most important for this thesis, affirms that electronic games must be conceived in light of respect for fundamental rights and democratic values, consumer protection, the full protection of children and adolescents, and the preservation of privacy, the protection of personal data<1>p. 544</1>
This is relevant because the framework does not enshrine a sectoral anything-goes dressed up as friendly modernity<1>p. 544</1>
Is a new law needed for platforms?

The way, then, is not to invent another law, nor to create parallel rules just for platforms. It is to adjust the reading of what is already written. What was missing were names capable of making certain losses visible, so that they can be shown, proved and claimed.
This also means that nothing here decides a case on its own. The tools exist, but each conflict still depends on what happened, on what can be shown and on how whoever decides reads the facts.

It is this shift that makes it possible to qualify the unlawful act of architecture without leaving the grammar of the CDC and without yielding to the temptation of inventing a parallel law for platforms.<1>p. 665</1>
This framework does not aim to mechanize the decision nor to reduce the complexity of the environment to a rigid formula.<1>p. 748</1>
<1>What you bought is a product, even with nothing in your hands</1><2>What you bought is a product, even with nothing in your hands</2>
When does what you bought depend on the platform?

When what you use depends, structurally, on an environment the platform administers, adjusts and can change. This is the case of the skin that only works inside the game and of the account that holds your inventory and your progress. What matters here is whether this dependence affects your access, your stay, how much you can understand what is happening or the updates to the experience.
What must the platform preserve?

Keeping what you bought accessible, understandable and preserved in what makes it useful. The platform can change the environment, because change is part of this kind of supply, but only within the limits of what is legitimate.
How to show what you bought and how you use it?

That what you use depends on the platform's environment and how it delivers this experience. It also helps to show your concrete position in the relationship, like what is in your account, what you paid and what that lets you do.
What if the company says it is just a service or a license?

That the case be handled under consumer law, with what you bought seen as an immaterial product. The company cannot escape this just by saying it provides a service or that it granted a simple license, because the service is precisely the way of keeping the product working.
Does recognizing the product already settle the case?

This is the first step, and not the end of the case. Recognizing the product opens the door to the other duties on this page, but each of them still depends on what happened to you. You do not need to fit every problem into this category to have protection.

Whenever the consumed utility depends structurally on an environment administered, modulated and made mutable by private governance, with impact on access, permanence, intelligibility or updating of the experience, the field of application of the IOC will be established.<1>p. 743</1>
The corresponding duty of supply is to ensure functionally accessible, intelligible and preserved enjoyment within the limits of the legitimate mutability of the environment.<1>p. 743</1>

The minimum required proof concerns the demonstration of the structural dependence of the utility on the governed ecosystem, of the way the experience is made available and of the consumer's concrete position in the bond.<1>p. 743</1>

The resulting legal qualification is that of an immaterial product subject to the regime of art. 3, § 1, of the CDC<1><2>3</2></1>, without the service dimension of the bond removing control of enjoyment as the core of the supply.<3>p. 743</3>

The possible institutional consequence consists in opening the subsequent filters of the regime, preventing the controversy from being neutralized by the claim of mere provision of a service or simple formal licensing.<1>p. 743</1>
The performance does not disappear, but appears as a mode of sustaining, updating and shaping the object of consumption itself.<1>p. 718</1>
All right, but when it goes wrong, what happens in practice?
