What if your skin changes tomorrow?
The same armor twice, side by side. The one on the left is whole. The one on the right has the same outline, but inside it is hollow, only the line of the drawing.

One day the update arrives. Your skin changes its appearance, gets another effect or loses an animation you liked. Or else the character it dresses is weakened and stops being worth it in matches, and almost nobody picks it anymore.

The skin is still in the account and the name is still the same. But what made it valuable, the fit with the rest of the game, with the story and with the recognition of other players, is no longer there. You have the same thing and, at the same time, you do not.

When an update alters appearance, effects, perceived rarity or economic insertion, the compatibility between experience, narrative and recognition may come undone. The promise of distinction remains nominally in the account, but no longer finds, in the world of the game, the fit that gave value to the investment of time, money and attention.<1>p. 104</1>
Does the contract let the company weaken what you bought?

This is provided for in the contract. The terms of use say that the company may alter, update, suspend and even weaken features of the service, including the virtual products you bought. They also say it may apply automatic patches, in the background, with or without notice.

And, in the game, strengthening and weakening are not an accident. They are the routine by which it is decided, in each update cycle, what is worth using and what is left behind for a while. Patches, character reworks, changes to visual effects and adjustments to the game's economy are not just technical maintenance, because they rewrite who stays, what is equivalent to what and what is recognized inside.

The Terms of Service state that the supplier may alter, update, suspend and even “nerf” features and parts of the services, including virtual products, in addition to providing for the application of background patches and automatic updates, with or without prior notice <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>.<3>p. 123</3>

In League of Legends, buffs and nerfs are not an accessory added after the game, but the very means by which the ecosystem defines, in regular cycles, which characters and strategies remain competitively viable and which are, for a period, downgraded to the condition of suboptimal choices<1>p. 121</1>

Patches, reworks, changes to visual effects and adjustments to the internal economy do not function merely as technical maintenance; they rewrite conditions of permanence, equivalence and recognition within the ecosystem.<1>p. 120</1>
Is game balance just a technical matter?
A real sequence took place in an online game. A character arrived in the game tied to the universe of a famous animated series, on a set date announced as a big moment.

Over the following year, her strength and the kind of defense she had became a constant topic in players' discussions and received successive technical interventions. At the end of the year, she got a prestige window, tied to a rare cosmetic, with a publicly announced opening date. And at the start of the next year an update replaced the core mechanism that protected her with a shield and expressly took away her damage immunity.

There is no need to guess the intention of whoever decided any of this. The sequence is enough to show that game balance is not just a technical matter. It also regulates who stays at the center, what is acceptable and how much each thing is worth, in step with the cycles of prestige and scarcity that the platform itself administers.
The official introduction of the character was presented as a narrative and temporal milestone associated with the Arcane universe, with an institutionally fixed release date<1>p. 131-132</1>

The episode involving the champion Mel makes it possible to observe, more sharply, how the technical rationality of balancing can operate coupled to the symbolic economy of the ecosystem, without the need to attribute subjective intention to the decision-maker.<1>p. 131</1>
First, her strength and the kind of defensive interaction her kit allowed became a recurring object of public evaluation and technical intervention<1>p. 132</1>
Second, already in the end-of-year cycle, this centrality was connected to a prestige window linked to rare cosmetic content, with a publicly recorded opening date<1>p. 132</1>

Then, at the start of 2026, patch 26.3 brought about a relevant respecification of the champion's mode of enjoyment by altering the core protection mechanism that sustained her pattern of interaction, replacing the previous logic with a shield and expressly removing damage immunity<1>p. 132</1>

The sequence is sufficient to support the view that design does not act merely as technical optimization, but as social mediation that regulates centrality, acceptability and functional value, including when this regulation is synchronized with cycles of prestige and scarcity administered by the platform itself<1>p. 132</1>
<1>Object and laboratory</1>Nerf

Nerf is the word players use for the deliberate weakening, done by update, of an attribute, an ability or an item. The character hits less, the item protects less, the ability takes longer to come back.

It is the clearest example of what this part shows. The name stays the same and access stays the same, while what you actually receive changes inside. And the permanence of the name comes to work as proof in favor of whoever made the change, because, at first sight, nothing has disappeared.

A privileged way of visualizing this loss of verifiability is the nerf, understood as the technically deliberate weakening of attributes, abilities or items, by means of a patch, to make something less powerful in the practical functioning of the game<1>p. 328</1>

The nerf is the limit case because it shows, with precision, how the continuity of the name and of access can work as self-justifying proof, while the relevant delivery shifts in what the environment counts as power and utility.<1>p. 329</1>

Now, an important caution. Not every change is a loss, and changing is not illegal. An online game needs to live. A new graphics engine, memory limits, loading times, compatibility with different computers and technical balance may require adjustments in the way the skin appears.

That is why the question is not whether the company can change something. It can. The question is under what conditions a change remains compatible with what was promised and with the value you bought.

And there is one more caution for those who bought a skin. A change in appearance only, as a rule, is not enough. It starts to matter when the symbolic value of the skin was part of the core of what was sold, or when the change adds up with other signs of a pattern that points to exploiting the user.
Mutability, in itself, is not unlawful.<1>p. 729</1>

Therefore, gradual changes to the graphics engine, the game's memory budget, loading routines and technical balance itself may, out of the need for performance and compatibility, modify the way the item presents itself<1>p. 439</1>
The question ceases to be whether changes are possible and becomes under what conditions they can be treated as compatible with the promise and with the preservation of relevant value.<1>p. 330</1>

Therefore, as a rule, predominantly aesthetic changes fall outside the reach of the concept, except when, in the concrete case, they form a convergent set of signs capable of supporting objective recognition of an unlawful act of architecture through structural indications of abusive teleology.<1>p. 434</1>
<1>Functional value equivalence</1>

To answer, there is a test. After the change, does the skin still play the same role in your experience? Does it serve what it served, occupy the same place among other players and, when that matters, still say what it said about you?

The test is demanding. It is not enough for the skin to keep working, nor to keep the same numbers in some isolated attribute. What counts is the role it had, and this includes utility, the relationship with others and, in certain cases, meaning. An item can remain in the account, open normally and still have lost what justified the purchase.

At the same time, nobody demands that nothing change, nor that the new version be identical to the old one. What is demanded is that the change not empty what was bought. Digital services change, but they cannot change in just any way.

What matters is the substantial preservation of the role played by the object in the acquired experience, considering its concrete utility in the ecosystem, its relational insertion in the environment of use and, when legally relevant, its identity or symbolic density.<1>p. 729</1>

Functional value equivalence is not reduced to the maintenance of technical performance in the strict sense, nor to the quantitative preservation of isolated attributes. Its content is more demanding.<1>p. 729</1>

The point is to affirm that the lawfulness of the change cannot be assessed merely by the nominal subsistence of the object, by the formal maintenance of access or by the abstract persistence of some residual utility.<1>p. 795</1>
This does not mean requiring perfect identity between the earlier and later versions, nor imposing a freeze on the service.<1>p. 730</1>

It allows us to recognize the sophisticated obvious: continuous digital services change, but they cannot change in just any way; IOCs evolve, but they cannot be emptied under the label of evolution<1>p. 655</1>
Was the change normal or did it empty what you bought?
Some questions help to separate a normal change from a change that empties what you bought.

Did the update remove an important function of the item? Did it weaken the item to the point that it lost the utility you paid to have? Did it change the screen in a way that disrupts everyday use? Did it redefine the rules so as to downgrade what had been promised as equivalent?

If any answer is yes, the change may have broken the equivalence. The platform could change things, but, in that case, it should have preserved the value of what you had or opened room for restoration, correction or review. And you do not need to prove you are the full owner of the item to complain about this. It is enough to show that the utility you acquired was arbitrarily downgraded.

The strength of the criterion appears sharply in cases such as removals of relevant functionalities, nerfs that empty acquired utility, interface changes that disrupt ordinary use, redefinitions of rules that downgrade the equivalence of what was promised<1>p. 637</1>

Functional value equivalence allows, precisely, a much more robust intermediate position: it is recognized that the platform may alter, but it is required that the alteration preserve, in substantial terms, the functional value of the acquired experience or, failing that, open room for restoration, correction, review or another adequate remedy<1>p. 637</1>
It is not necessary to demonstrate full dominion over the object to maintain that the acquired enjoyment cannot be arbitrarily downgraded.<1>p. 637</1>
What pattern forms when the skin gets worse and stays in the account?
The pattern that forms is this. The worsened skin does not leave the scene. It stays there, weaker, less central and less useful, or less equivalent to what justified the purchase.

You did not lose a detail. You lost part of what you bought and, often, you are pushed to look for something else in the same store, to recover what you had. It is extraction by attrition, in which the company profits from the erosion of what it has already sold. The thing exists, but existing is not the same as remaining what you bought.

Nerfs, reconfigurations, balancing adjustments, gradual suppressions of function, shifts of utility to new layers of acquisition and ordinary redefinitions of equivalence operate as techniques of extraction by erosion. The object does not leave the scene entirely. It remains there, but worsened, weaker, less central, less useful or less equivalent to what justified the acquisition.<1>p. 672</1>
The consumer does not lose merely “a feature”; they lose functional substance of what they bought and are often pushed to seek substitutes within the same ecosystem.<1>p. 672</1>
An object may continue to exist and, even so, no longer be, in a legally relevant sense, what was acquired.<1>p. 795</1>
<1>Law</1>Captive contracts

Why not simply accept it and move on? Because, in a relationship that lasts for years, you are not that free to say no. Someone who has already invested time and money, and depends on the game to keep using what they have, accepts the change because leaving would cost more. In these long contracts, the yes that comes later is often just forced adherence to the new state of things.

That is why the freedom to contract has limits when the contract lasts over time. The power to change the performance cannot be used to frustrate the function that justified the purchase. And the Consumer Protection Code already says, clearly, that a clause letting the supplier change on its own the content or quality of what it delivers after the contract is made is void.

[...] but because it helps to visualize something that continuous digital consumption lays wide open: performance is not exhausted in the initial adherence, and the bond comes to be structured by practical dependence, permanent asymmetry, sedimented trust and the supplier's renewed power of imposition over time<1>p. 559</1>

In captive contracts, the so-called supervening “consent” is often nothing more than forced adherence to the new state of affairs, especially when the consumer is already invested in the relationship and depends on the ecosystem to keep enjoying what they acquired.<1>p. 654-655</1>

Contractual freedom finds limits in the social function of the contract, and, in continued consumer relationships, this limitation takes a very concrete form: the power to alter, modulate or reconfigure the performance cannot be exercised so as to frustrate the function that justified the consumer's original acquisition<1>p. 561</1>

On the most classic plane of the CDC, this prohibition already appears sufficiently clearly. A clause authorizing unilateral modification of the content or quality of the performance after contracting is void<1>p. 561</1>

Now try to prove what changed. You would need to show when the change happened, by what criterion and with what effect on what you had. But whoever keeps the system records, the old versions, the histories and the reasons for each decision is the platform.

Whoever controls these traces controls, in large part, the reconstruction of what happened. And, as long as you cannot show the difference, the continuity of the name and of the signs serves as proof for the other side.

Whoever controls logs, histories, decision criteria, relevant versions, interface records, moderation flows, alteration parameters and traces of sanction controls, to a large extent, the conditions for the legal reconstruction of what happened.<1>p. 734</1>

Without this minimum, the dispute tends to be resolved by surface and impression, because the continuity of signs works as self-justifying proof while the consumer cannot demonstrate what changed, by which criteria and with what effect on the acquired position<1>p. 326</1>
<1>Open auditability</1>

The platform cannot change what you use and, at the same time, keep in absolute secrecy what changed, when it changed, why it changed, what effect this had and which records make it possible to reconstruct the case. This duty is not a new law with a name of its own. It comes from the duty to inform, from good faith and from making the consumer's defense easier, which the law already provides for, and it serves so that the change can be verified.

Nor is it a matter of opening the game's code or handing over the company's secrets. What is asked for is a minimum that can be demonstrated, enough to see whether there was a relevant change, link it to what was promised and check whether it was justified. It is sufficient transparency, and not total transparency.

And there is a limit. This duty does not arise with any small adjustment or change in appearance only. It begins when the change truly affects what you use, your stay or your chance to prove and contest.

In other words, the platform cannot claim to alter the regime of enjoyment and, at the same time, keep in absolute secrecy what it actually altered, when it altered it, why it altered it, what relevant effects the change produces and which records make it possible to reconstruct the episode in case of conflict<1>p. 636</1>

A standard of minimum verifiability, compatible with the protection of software and trade secrets, but incompatible with the opaque shielding of performance; an unfolding of the duty to inform, of objective good faith and of facilitating the consumer's defense<1>p. 648</1>

The standard does not require exposure of industrial secrets as a purifying fetish. It requires, rather, a demonstrable minimum capable of preventing information, good faith and transparency from turning into empty performances.<1>p. 636</1>

What is needed is sufficient intelligibility to identify the occurrence of a relevant change, relate it to the promised enjoyment, verify whether there was a justification compatible with the legal regime<1>p. 728</1>
Not total transparency, but sufficient transparency.<1>p. 728</1>
Open auditability is not demandable in the face of any microscopic adjustment, any cosmetic change or any irrelevant fluctuation of the service.<1>p. 642</1>

And the frustration you feel? If the platform promised value, rarity, performance or advantage, and then downgraded everything by criteria nobody sees, this frustration is not a mere annoyance. It may be the sign that the delivery itself failed, and so it may carry legal weight.

If the platform promises a curated experience of value, rarity, performance or advantage, and then rebalances or downgrades it under opaque criteria, the frustration is not mere displeasure. It may be a relevant inadequacy of the governed enjoyment itself.<1>p. 634</1>
<1>A relevant change needs to leave a trail</1><2>A relevant change needs to leave a trail</2>
When does a change need to leave a trail?

When the platform changes something important in your access, in the item's performance, in its utility or in the rules of the game, or when it applies a punishment. And it does this without keeping the minimum record needed to reconstruct what happened. This is the case of the item that loses strength in an update with no explanation that can be checked, or of the account suspended without anyone knowing on what basis.
What trail must the platform keep?
Maintaining a minimum of verifiability, which means making it possible to know what was changed, when, with what justification and with what effect on what you use.

This duty is not a new law with a name of its own. It comes from the duty to inform, from good faith and from making the consumer's defense easier, which the law already provides for. It does not require opening all of the game's code nor making the company's secrets public. The examination should be limited to what matters for the case, preserving the necessary confidentiality.
Which records make it possible to understand the change or the punishment?

The essential system records, the history of the versions that matter, the records of the punishment and the minimum justifications. Together with the context data, this should be enough for whoever will decide to understand the problem. Almost all of this is usually with the platform, and not with you.
What to ask for to reconstruct the change?

That these records be preserved and shown and that there be an expert examination, carried out by a specialist, on defined points. That it be verified, based on the minimum clarity the platform owes, whether the change or the punishment was legitimate. Depending on the case, there may also be presumptions against the platform, which make certain facts count in your favor when the records only it had are missing.
Does every small adjustment require a record?

It is not every small adjustment, change in appearance only or unimportant fluctuation that requires this trail. The duty begins when the change relevantly affects what you use, your stay or your chance to prove and contest.

Whenever relevant changes of access, performance, utility, operating rule or sanction affect enjoyment without the preservation of minimum trails for institutional reconstruction, there will be a violation of the open auditability parameter.<1>p. 745</1>

The corresponding duty of supply is to maintain minimum verifiability over what was altered, when it was altered, on what grounds it was justified and what functionally relevant effects it produced.<1>p. 745</1>
It is for this reason that open auditability must be understood as an internal unfolding of the duty to inform and not as an institution foreign to the microsystem.<1>p. 641</1>
The requirement of open auditability is not to be confused with full opening of the source code nor with suppression of the technical confidentiality of the software.<1>p. 643</1>

The minimum required proof consists of essential logs, history of relevant versions, sanction records, minimum operational justifications, context data and delimited technical elements sufficient to make the controversy cognizable.<1>p. 745</1>

The institutional consequence includes orders for preservation and display of records, delimited expert examination, presumptions unfavorable to the supplier and review of the lawfulness of the alteration or sanction based on minimum institutional intelligibility.<1>p. 745</1>

It may affect access and permanence, the functional integrity of the object, promised equivalences, the symbolic position of the IOC in the ecosystem, or even the consumer's conditions of proof and contestation.<1>p. 642</1>
<1>If it changed, it has to keep what it was worth</1><2>If it changed, it has to keep what it was worth</2>
When does the update take away the function of what you bought?

When the platform changes the experience in a way that truly worsens, empties or diverts the function that led you to buy. It is the item that, after an adjustment, remains in the inventory but became so weak that it lost its reason to exist, or the feature that let you do something and was removed.
You may remain inside the game, with the account, seeing the item and logging in whenever you want, and still have lost the main thing. Keeping it working is not the same as keeping its value.
What must the platform preserve in the item?

Preserving, in what is substantial, the role the item had in your experience. This includes what it does, the relationship it creates with other players and, when this matters for the law, what it means.
How to show what changed in the item's utility?
What utility the item had before, what changed, what the concrete impact of the change was and why the compensation offered, if any, is not enough.
What solution can restore the lost utility?

First, that the function come back. This may mean undoing the change when technically possible, replacing the item with something equivalent or correcting the way the update was made. Money should not be the automatic answer. Depending on the case, the loss may be treated as a defect in the quality of the product or service, which is the name the law gives to the problem that makes something less useful than it should be.
Is the game forbidden to change?

The platform can update the game, and nobody demands that the item stay identical forever nor that the game stand still in time. Many changes are, in fact, the natural evolution of the environment. The problem is the change that throws onto you the cost of seriously worsening what you bought, without a fitting restoration.

Whenever the platform alters the experience so as to substantially degrade, empty or divert the function that justified the acquisition, there will be a rupture of functional value equivalence.<1>p. 745</1>
The strength of the criterion appears sharply in cases such as removals of relevant functionalities, nerfs that empty acquired utility<1>p. 637</1>

The consumer remains formally “inside” the ecosystem, still has the account, still sees the object, can still access the platform. Even so, the enjoyed utility may be substantially downgraded<1>p. 635</1>
The corresponding duty of supply is to preserve, in substantial terms, the functional, relational and, when legally relevant, symbolic role of the object in the consumer's experience.<1>p. 745</1>

The minimum required proof calls for demonstration of the utility previously incorporated into the bond, of the change that occurred, of the concrete functional impact of the alteration and of the insufficiency of any restoration offered.<1>p. 745-746</1>
The possible legal qualification tends to fall on a defect in the quality of the product or service<1>p. 746</1>

The possible institutional consequence prioritizes functional restoration, technical reversal when feasible, equivalent replacement and correction of the form of updating, instead of mere automatic monetization of the loss.<1>p. 746</1>

What the parameter rejects is not change itself, but its instrumentalization to transfer to the consumer the cost of reconfigurations that destroy or significantly downgrade the acquired utility without compatible restoration.<1>p. 730</1>

Nerfs, removals, reworks, migrations, rule changes, reordering of access, reconfiguration of interfaces and suppression of functionalities are usually narrated as the natural evolution of the environment. In many cases, they may in fact be so.<1>p. 730</1>

And when it goes wrong?
A hand returns the missing piece to a mosaic, while a pile of coins sits to the side, unused.
Let's say your skin lost what it had. Or that your account was closed for a reason you cannot understand. The first problem that shows up is proof.

The system records, the old versions of the screens, the criteria used to punish, the history of changes and the internal support conversations are all on the other side. In conflicts of this kind, this is the normal situation, and not an exception. When the proof arises and stays under the platform's control, the proceedings cannot pretend that both parties stand on an equal footing.

In disputes over IOCs, this is precisely the normal configuration: logs, interface trails, change histories, sanction criteria, internal support communications and relevant technical records are concentrated with the supplier.<1>p. 659</1>
When the proof arises and remains under the platform's control, the procedural system cannot pretend neutrality.<1>p. 659</1>
What can you yourself keep as proof?

What is within your reach is more than it seems. Dated screenshots, screen recordings, the purchase and confirmation screens and the messages about rarity, time remaining, discount, event or change show how the environment was put together. It also helps to keep what was promised, like ads, posts and notices, to compare with what you received later.

The difference is big. You stop saying only that you did not understand and start showing that the environment was designed in a certain way. What counts is not your memory, but the shape the platform gave to the path you traveled.

The first source of support is interface trails and decision flow: dated screenshots, screen recordings, purchase, acceptance, upgrade and confirmation screens, messages about rarity, equivalence, time remaining, discount, event or change<1>p. 607</1>

What is relevant there is not the user's subjective memory, but the architecture actually presented. The claim ceases to be “I did not understand” and becomes “the environment was designed this way”.<1>p. 607</1>
The advertising and institutional promise is compared with the enjoyment actually delivered and with its later changes.<1>p. 607</1>
And when all the proof is with the company?

And the law already has tools for the rest. One of them is the reversal of the burden of proof. Normally, whoever alleges a fact needs to prove it. In a consumer relationship, the judge can shift this weight in favor of the consumer. And, when the service is very technical and the supplier controls everything, this reversal is often the only way for protection to work.

There are others. The judge can order the platform to keep the evidence and produce documents. And the judge can divide the work of proving in another way when one party has great difficulty and the other has great ease in producing the proof.

None of this is automatic. Some argue that the reversal should always apply, for every digital relationship, but today it depends on the judge's assessment in the case. That is why you still need to tell a coherent story that seems true, and make clear what you are disputing. What changes is that you cannot be required to give detailed proof of something that was never in your hands. And, to begin with, you do not need the game's entire code. A minimum is enough, like comparing the before and after and showing what was affected.

The technological specialization of the service and the dominant position of the supplier make the reversal of the burden of proof, in many cases, the only instrument capable of effectively enabling consumer protection<1>p. 583</1>
The third mechanism is properly procedural: preservation of evidence, production of documents and dynamic redistribution of the burden of proof.<1>p. 659</1>

Art. 373, § 1, allows a different distribution of the burden of proof when there is excessive difficulty for one party to discharge the burden or greater ease for the other to produce proof of the contrary fact<1>p. 659</1>

[...] which is why digital vulnerability and the corresponding hyposufficiency should be affirmed in a universal key, with reversal of the burden of proof ope legis, and not only ope judicis<1>p. 593</1>
This does not eliminate the need for plausibility, for argumentative sequencing or for delimitation of the disputed object.<1>p. 736</1>

The more the reconstruction of the conflict depends on internal governance, the less reasonable it will be to require from the consumer a detailed demonstration of facts whose documentary and technical support was never within their reach.<1>p. 736</1>

The minimum signal of proof requires a functional comparison between before and after, examination of relevant versions, identification of the affected core of utility and assessment of the object's role in the experience<1>p. 672</1>
Who pays when fraud goes through an official game function?

There is a case that shows how the risk can land in your lap. In an online game, sending gifts to friends was an official function, which the company itself offered inside the game, with rules and limits. At the same time, outside stores sold the game's currency as something normal, safe and advantageous, and nobody made clear what was allowed, tolerated or forbidden.

When card fraud appeared, the company switched off the gift function in Brazil for a long period, removed items received and blocked accounts or rolled them back to an earlier state. The measure also hit those who had received gifts in good faith, unaware of any fraud. And those who lost skins were left with the task of proving, item by item, where each one came from, with old statements, emails and screenshots they might have kept.

The case helps to understand three things. The company already knew the risk of fraud, and so this risk is part of its activity and cannot be treated as the fault of whoever received the gift. A revocable license in the contract is not enough to throw the system's failure onto you. And from this arise concrete requests, like returning what was removed when no individual proof rules out your good faith, keeping and showing the records and correcting the information about where to buy safely.

On the contrary, Riot itself presented it as a regular functionality, integrated into the game client, subject to objective eligibility requirements, quantitative limits, regional restrictions and standardized sending flows<1>p. 610</1>
promotional materials and digital storefronts presented the external purchase of virtual currency as an ordinary, safe, advantageous practice compatible with the game's ecosystem<1>p. 612</1>
The vulnerability does not stem from private naivety, but from the absence of robust communicational demarcation between what was admitted, tolerated, official or forbidden.<1>p. 612</1>

In this environment, it is not legally serious to presume that the average consumer would always distinguish, with sufficient clarity, a tolerated partner, legitimate resale, gray market and fraud linked to a cloned card<1>p. 612</1>

The company deactivated the gift functionality on the Brazilian server for a long period, suppressed assets received and carried out regressive restorations or blocks on affected accounts<1>p. 611</1>

[...] it suppressed assets, interrupted an official content circulation functionality and applied sanctions based on broad presumptions of co-responsibility, including on users who did not knowingly take part in the fraud<1>p. 610</1>

Once the assets are removed or the account state is reverted, the user comes to depend on old statements, scattered emails, past screenshots and reconstructed memory to prove that a given content legitimately formed part of their position of enjoyment<1>p. 616</1>

The episode shows how the platform, by carrying out a broad reversion of the account state, transfers to the player the almost archaeological burden of reconstructing item by item what was already part of their sphere of enjoyment<1>p. 616</1>
It was an institutionally recognized operational risk, with internal flows for investigation, refund and suspension<1>p. 610</1>
The risk comes to form part of the professional circle of the economic operation itself.<1>p. 611</1>
The central dogmatic point, however, is that this contractual vocabulary is not enough to convert the consumer into the legitimate recipient of systemic risk.<1>p. 615</1>

The consumer regime admits, here, requests for functional restoration of the position of enjoyment, restoration of assets when the user's good faith has not been refuted by robust individualized proof, preservation and display of minimum records of the supply, informational correction about legitimate channels of acquisition<1>p. 617</1>
<1>Functional restoration</1><2><3>Functional restoration</3></2>

And what is asked for, in the end? Before money, that what was taken be returned. This may mean restoring your access, reviewing or undoing the punishment and giving back to the skin the function it had. It may also mean preserving your history, offering a substitute that plays the same role and correcting the procedure that caused the problem.

The reason is simple. When what you lost was the possibility of continuing to use something, compensation alone is usually a poor remedy. It puts a number in place of the loss, but it does not give back the account, the history or the place you had in the game.
In cases of architectural injury, the legal response must favor functional restoration and procedural correction, instead of automatically resorting to monetization.<1>p. 751</1>

[...] the integrity of the experience, the permanence of access, the intelligibility of the bond or the consumer's relational position in the ecosystem, a simple monetary award tends to operate as a poor and structurally ineffective remedy<1>p. 751</1>

What is required, whenever possible, is restoration of access, reversal or review of sanctions, restoration of functionality, preservation of history, equivalent replacement and adjustment of governance procedures.<1>p. 751</1>
Does money leave the scene?

Money does not leave the scene. Compensation remains legitimate and often indispensable, whether to cover material losses or to recognize harms that are not only material. It just stops being the automatic answer, as if every loss of this kind could become a number on a spreadsheet, without anyone looking at what was lost.

Sometimes your case is only a symptom. If the same design produces the same loss in series, fixing your case does not solve it, because tomorrow the loss happens to someone else, or to you again.

In these cases, the response needs to reach the source. This opens room for orders that prevent repetition, for changes in the structure of the service, for collective actions and for mandatory compliance mechanisms, linked to the duty to make changes verifiable. Without this, the law only puts a price on the harm and leaves intact the machine that produces it.

Regime correction, on the contrary, makes it possible to treat the harm as architectural and not merely as an episode. With this, it becomes possible to justify injunctive relief, structural measures, collective measures and even mandatory compliance mechanisms compatible with open auditability and institutional control of enjoyment.<1>p. 741</1>
The primacy of functional restoration and regime correction prevents consumer protection from limiting itself to pricing harms while keeping intact the machine that produces them.<1>p. 742</1>
